A deadlock is when two or more threads (or processes) are each waiting for a resource another one holds, so none can ever proceed. The classic case: thread A holds lock 1 and wants lock 2, while thread B holds lock 2 and wants lock 1.

It requires four conditions at once: mutual exclusion (the resource can't be shared), hold-and-wait (a thread keeps what it has while waiting for more), no preemption (locks can't be taken away), and circular wait (a cycle of threads each waiting on the next). Break any one and deadlock is impossible.

The most practical fix is to break circular wait by always acquiring locks in the same global order everywhere in the code. If every thread takes lock 1 before lock 2, no cycle can form.

When ordering isn't feasible, use a try-lock with a timeout and release everything on failure before retrying, which breaks hold-and-wait. Beyond that, hold locks for as short a time as possible, avoid calling unknown code (callbacks, I/O) while holding one, and prefer fewer locks or lock-free designs such as message passing or immutable data, since a thread that holds only one lock at a time cannot deadlock.
